title: The Seers Who Heard the Vedas
hook: who wrote the Vedas? the creation hymn shows the seers at work, stretching a line across the dark
carry: the vedas were heard by seers, not invented
tomorrow: even the gods came later. so who really knows how it began?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fourth verse of the Nasadiya Sukta: kama, desire, the first seed of mind, and poets searching their hearts for the bond of what is in what is not.

Who wrote the Vedas? Ask a Hindu grandmother and you may get a surprising answer: nobody wrote them. They were heard. Yesterday the Rig Veda's creation hymn showed poets searching their hearts for where everything came from, and finding the bond of what is in what is not. Today's verse shows what those seers did next. They stretched a line across the dark, and then, right away, they asked about it.
screen: `WHO WROTE THE VEDAS?` → `POETS SEARCHING THEIR HEARTS.` → `A LINE ACROSS THE DARK.`

segments.voice: The fifth verse of the Nasadiya Sukta, in paraphrase: their cord was stretched across. Was there something below it? Was there something above it? There were seed-placers, there were great powers: their own power below, a giving forth above. The word for cord is rashmi: a ray, a rein, a line. Whose cord? The verse says only 'their'. Many readers take it to be the poets of the verse before, the ones who searched their hearts, so their insight is the line drawn across the dark. And even while they describe, they ask: was there below? was there above? Here a big Hindu teaching comes into view. Hindus call the Vedas shruti, what was heard. Tradition calls the rishis seers of the mantras: they didn't invent the hymns at a desk, they saw and heard them in deep attention, and handed them on mouth to ear, teacher to student, sound for sound. That's why the Vedas were kept by chanting for many centuries before anyone relied on writing them down, and why a family still calls a pandit who learned them by heart. In this verse you can watch the seers at work: looking inward, drawing a line, and honestly asking about both sides. It's the same reason a child in a Hindu home often learns a prayer by ear from a grandparent long before she can read it. So when a friend asks who wrote your scripture, here's a Hindu answer: in our telling, seers heard it, and we keep it by sound.
screen: `RASHMI: A CORD, A RAY, A LINE.` · `WAS THERE BELOW? WAS THERE ABOVE?` · `SHRUTI: HANDED ON MOUTH TO EAR.` · `SEERS HEARD IT; WE KEEP IT.`

segments.voice: Vedic recitation traditionally begins with Om, so begin there. Sit easily and chant Om softly three times, or say it in your mind, letting the sound fade each time; then sit in the quiet after it and listen, the way the seers are pictured listening, not making anything up, just hearing. If you pray, let the quiet be prayer; if you don't, simply listen.
The Nasadiya Sukta. The hymn of creation. In its fifth verse, the seers stretch a line across the dark, and ask about both sides of it.
Your line: the Vedas were heard by seers, not invented. And even their line got a question on each side. See you tomorrow.
